![Image from [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.07972). Figure 1 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](cover.jpg){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="cover-full.jpg"}

In *Adaptive Collaboration with Humans: Metacognitive Policy Optimization for Multi-Agent LLMs with Continual Learning* (ICLR 2026 Poster) [[1]](#ref-1), [Wei Yang](https://www.semanticscholar.org/author/Wei-Yang/2270893841), [Defu Cao](https://defucao.github.io/), Jiacheng Pang, Muyan Weng, and [Yan Liu](https://viterbi-web.usc.edu/~yanliu/) (USC) train each agent in a multi-agent system to choose one of three high-level actions at each round (Evaluate a peer's answer, Create a new one, Defer to a human expert) and turn deferral events into supervised data for continual capability growth.

> While scaling individual Large Language Models (LLMs) has delivered remarkable progress, the next frontier lies in scaling collaboration through multi-agent systems (MAS). However, purely autonomous MAS remain "closed-world" systems, constrained by the static knowledge horizon of pre-trained models. This limitation makes them brittle on tasks requiring knowledge beyond training data, often leading to collective failure under novel challenges. To address this, we propose the *Human-In-the-Loop Multi-Agent Collaboration (HILA)* framework, a principled paradigm for human–agent collaboration. HILA trains agents to learn a *metacognitive policy that governs when to solve problems autonomously and when to defer to a human expert*. To operationalize this policy, we introduce *Dual-Loop Policy Optimization*, which disentangles immediate decision-making from long-term capability growth. The inner loop applies Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a cost-aware reward to optimize deferral decisions, while the outer loop implements *continual learning, transforming expert feedback into high-quality supervised signals* that strengthen the agent's reasoning ability. Experiments on challenging mathematical and problem-solving benchmarks show that HILA, equipped with Dual-Loop Policy Optimization, *consistently outperforms advanced MAS*, establishing a principled foundation for collaborative and continually improving agentic systems.

## Methods

HILA (Human-In-the-Loop Multi-Agent Collaboration) models human-agent collaboration as a Metacognitive [Markov Decision Process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_decision_process) (Meta-MDP). At each round $t$, every agent $i$ observes a shared state $s_t = \text{concat}(\mathbf{x}^{\text{task}}_t, \mathbf{x}^{\text{self}}_t, \mathbf{x}^{\text{peer}}_t, \mathbf{z}^{\text{soc}}_t, \mathbf{z}^{\text{mon}}_t, \mathbf{z}^{\text{ctrl}}_t)$ — task context, self context, peer context, plus three optional cognitive cues (social consensus, metacognitive monitoring, cognitive control) computed from interaction traces with rule-based heuristics. The action space is a discrete set of three high-level strategies: $a^{\text{eval}}$ endorses an existing peer answer, $a^{\text{create}}$ generates a new candidate, and $a^{\text{defer}}$ routes the round's output to a human expert.

Dual-Loop Policy Optimization (DLPO) [[1]](#ref-1) trains the policy with two coupled loops. The **inner loop** teaches the agent which of the three actions to pick at each round. The reward pays the agent for getting the answer right and charges it a small fee for creating a new answer, a larger fee for calling the human, so the policy learns to defer only when the expected accuracy gain outweighs the cost. Formally, this is Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [[4]](#ref-4) on a cost-aware reward, with $C_{\text{defer}} > C_{\text{create}} \geq 0$:

$$R(s_t, a_t) = \begin{cases} R_{\text{gt}}(\hat{y}(a_t)), & a_t = \text{EVAL} \\ R_{\text{gt}}(\hat{y}(a_t)) - C_{\text{create}}, & a_t = \text{CREATE} \\ R_{\text{gt}}(\hat{y}_{\text{human}}(a_t)) - C_{\text{defer}}, & a_t = \text{DEFER} \end{cases}$$

Correctness $R_{\text{gt}}$ is the primary signal. The two cost terms break ties toward the cheaper action when multiple choices lead to similar outcomes. GRPO turns these rewards into a learning signal by sampling several actions at the same state, comparing each one's reward against the group's average, and pushing the policy toward the actions that beat the average. The advantage $A(s_t, a_k) = R(s_t, a_k) - \tfrac{1}{K}\sum_j R(s_t, a_j)$ feeds the policy-gradient term $\mathcal{L}_{\text{PG}}$, which scales each action's log-probability by its advantage. Two regularizers stabilize training: $\mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}}$ is the KL divergence between the current policy and the initial reference policy (keeps the trained policy close to its starting point so it doesn't drift off into degenerate behaviors), and $\mathcal{L}_{\text{Entropy}}$ is the policy's entropy over the three actions (subtracted to *encourage* spread, preventing collapse onto a single action). The combined inner objective is $\mathcal{L}_{\text{Inner}} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{PG}} + \beta_{\text{kl}} \mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}} - \beta_{\text{ent}} \mathcal{L}_{\text{Entropy}}$.

The **outer loop** runs continual supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on every deferral event. Each time the agent calls the human, the human's answer is recorded as a training example, and the generator is later fine-tuned to produce that answer itself given the same context. Over many deferrals the agent absorbs the human's expertise on cases it could not handle, so future encounters with similar problems no longer need a deferral. Formally, the human's response $y_{\text{human}} = (t_1, \dots, t_L)$ becomes a target sequence trained with token-level cross-entropy:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}(\theta) = -\sum_{i=1}^{L} \log \pi_\theta(t_i \mid s_t, t_{1:i-1}).$$

The two losses share parameters and are combined under an indicator that gates SFT to deferral steps only:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{(s_t, a_t)}\left[\mathcal{L}_{\text{Inner}}(\theta) + \lambda_{\text{sft}} \cdot \mathbb{I}(a_t = a^{\text{defer}}) \cdot \mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}(\theta)\right].$$

The inner loop decides *when* to defer. The outer loop teaches the generator *what* the human said when it did.

![Accuracy versus deferral rate on GSM8K across the three training stages (Init policy, +GRPO inner loop, +DLPO with continual outer loop). DLPO moves the operating point up and to the left simultaneously: higher accuracy with lower reliance on the human expert. Figure 6 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](figure6.png){fig-align="center"}

## Results

The paper evaluates HILA on five benchmarks spanning math reasoning (GSM8K [[5]](#ref-5), AMC, AIME), code generation (HumanEval [[6]](#ref-6)), and general knowledge (MMLU [[7]](#ref-7)), with LLaMA3-8B as the main backbone and ablations on LLaMA3-3B and Qwen2.5-3B. The primary metric is task accuracy. Deferral rate (the fraction of rounds that call the human) is reported as the cost dimension. Baselines split into single-agent prompting strategies — Chain-of-Thought (CoT) [[8]](#ref-8), Self-Consistency (SC) [[9]](#ref-9) — and multi-agent systems — Progressive Hint Prompting (PHP) [[10]](#ref-10) (classified as MA in the paper, framed as a pairwise/pooled critique baseline), LLM-Debate [[11]](#ref-11), GroupDebate (G-Debate) [[12]](#ref-12), DyLAN [[13]](#ref-13), GPTSwarm (G-Swarm) [[14]](#ref-14), AgentPrune (A-Prune) [[15]](#ref-15), and AFlow [[16]](#ref-16). The "Vanilla" reference is the backbone with no agentic scaffolding. Headline numbers come from Table 1. Cross-backbone scaling and ablations live in Tables 2 and 4, and the cost-sensitivity sweep is Figure 11(a).

![Table 1 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1). Main comparison on the LLaMA3-8B backbone across GSM8K, AMC, AIME, HumanEval, and MMLU. Parenthesized values are absolute deltas vs the Vanilla baseline. Underlines mark the best non-HILA entry per benchmark. SA = single-agent, MA = multi-agent.](table1.png){fig-align="center"}

- **HILA tops every benchmark over every baseline** — single-agent (CoT, SC) and multi-agent (PHP, LLM-Debate, G-Debate, DyLAN, G-Swarm, A-Prune, AFlow). The runner-up varies by task (G-Swarm on GSM8K, G-Debate on AMC and MMLU, AFlow on HumanEval), but no single multi-agent baseline wins anything.
- **Big gains on hard reasoning, AIME ceiling**: HumanEval +24.59 over Vanilla, AMC +24.47, GSM8K +17.10, MMLU +15.63, AIME +6.41. Deferral pays off most on AMC and HumanEval. The modest AIME gain suggests the human proxy itself struggles there, capping the upside.
- **Cross-backbone story (Table 2 in the paper)**: the absolute gain grows as the backbone weakens. On LLaMA3-3B, HILA lifts GSM8K from 45.26 to 83.85 (+38.59), the largest gain of any base model tested.
- **Inner-loop vs outer-loop (Table 4 ablation, LLaMA3-8B)**: HILA Init Policy (the unoptimized HILA system, before any training) starts at 88.15/33.33/68.30 (GSM8K/AMC/MMLU). GRPO inner-loop alone adds +0.23/-0.83/+2.17 (flat on GSM8K, mild AMC regression, real MMLU lift). Full DLPO with continual-SFT outer-loop lifts +1.71/+2.50/+5.32 over Init Policy.
- **Cost-sensitivity** (Figure 11(a) below): as the deferral cost $C_{\text{defer}}$ rises, the policy defers less and accuracy degrades gracefully. The same trained model serves a range of operating points without re-fitting.

![Accuracy on AMC and MMLU under different deferral costs $C_{\text{defer}}$. As deferral becomes more expensive, the policy defers less and accuracy degrades gracefully. The meta-policy is calibrated to the cost rather than fixed. Figure 11(a) from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](figure9.png){fig-align="center"}

## My Notes

- **"Inner/outer" suggests nesting that isn't there.** In meta-learning and bilevel optimization, the naming usually marks a nested solver structure: an inner loop runs to convergence (or partial convergence) per outer step, often against separate parameters or objectives. HILA's actual training objective is $\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{Inner}} + \lambda \cdot \mathbb{I}(a=\text{defer}) \cdot \mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}$. That's a sum of two terms with shared parameters, gated by an indicator, updated together each step. The time-scale separation is genuine: per-round decisions accumulate to feed SFT updates over training. Beyond that, there's no nesting. Plainer labels like "policy loss + SFT loss" or "decisions plus demonstrations" would map more directly to what the equations do.
- **Cost-aware abstention.** The missing piece in most "calibration" work. [Kadavath's "Mostly Know"](/posts/20260504-kadavath-mostly-know/) [[2]](#ref-2) measures whether a model's confidence tracks its correctness, but stops short of prescribing what the model should do when confidence is low. HILA closes the loop by making deferral a first-class action with an explicit price tag. The cost-sensitivity sweep in Figure 11(a), where accuracy degrades gracefully as $C_{\text{defer}}$ increases, is the part most production deployments need: a single knob that maps a budget into an operating point.
- **Defer-event SFT is weaker intrinsic metacognition.** [Liu and van der Schaar](/posts/20260430-intrinsic-metacognitive-learning/) [[3]](#ref-3) argued that genuine self-improvement requires the agent to decide *what to learn* and *how to evaluate* its learning, not just execute a designer-defined loop. HILA's outer loop is an extrinsic mechanism, with the trigger (defer event), the target (human's answer), the loss (SFT), and the schedule all wired in. What the outer loop gets right is the data-curation half: the agent's own metacognitive policy decides which examples enter the SFT set. That's a step toward intrinsic metacognition, but every other part of the loop is still hand-designed.
- **Strongest gain, weakest base.** On LLaMA3-3B, HILA lifts GSM8K from 45.26 to 83.85 (+38.59), against DyLAN's +30.91 and GPTSwarm's +26.59 on the same base. Two readings: (i) deferral is most valuable when the base policy is most likely to be wrong, which is the right scaling direction for an "open-world" claim, and (ii) the comparison is partly unfair to the autonomous baselines, which have no human oracle to defer to. The paper counts Defer as an action with a cost, but the missing experiment is DyLAN with the same human-call budget HILA spends. The Vanilla-DLPO ablation on LLaMA3-8B (72.76 → 82.11 on GSM8K) isolates the SFT contribution but doesn't match budgets either.

## Related Posts

- [Truly Self-Improving Agents Require Intrinsic Metacognitive Learning](/posts/20260430-intrinsic-metacognitive-learning/): the framework that grades HILA's defer-event SFT as still-extrinsic metacognition, with the trigger and loss hand-designed.
- [Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know](/posts/20260504-kadavath-mostly-know/): measures whether confidence tracks correctness but stops short of prescribing action, which HILA's cost-aware deferral supplies.
- [ReMA: Learning to Meta-think for LLMs with Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning](/posts/20260430-rema-meta-think/): another multi-agent RL split into high- and low-level roles, a methodological sibling to HILA's deferral meta-policy.
- [Multi-Agent Design: Optimizing Agents with Better Prompts and Topologies](/posts/20260430-multi-agent-system-search/): an alternative axis for improving multi-agent systems — search over prompts and topology rather than a learned deferral policy.
- [MAST: A Failure Taxonomy for Multi-Agent Systems](/posts/20250802-mast-multi-agent-failures/): catalogs why autonomous multi-agent systems fail collectively, the brittleness HILA's human-in-the-loop deferral targets.
